name: Design a Payment System
intent: Charge customers through an outside provider so that money moves exactly once, every cent is accounted for, and nothing is lost when a call times out or a server crashes.
codeTitle: charging exactly once and recording balanced ledger entries
finalIntro: One payment from checkout to settlement, including the reply that gets lost on the way.
prompt: Design the payment backend of an online shop. A customer presses Pay, the shop charges their card through a payment provider, and the order is confirmed. Money must never be charged twice or lost, and the shop must always be able to explain where every cent went.
functional: Create a payment for an order and charge the customer's card through a provider
Show the customer a clear result: paid, failed, or still processing
Refund all or part of a payment
Keep a record of every money movement for accounting and support
Tell the rest of the shop (orders, email, invoices) when a payment succeeds or fails
nonFunctional: Never charge a customer twice for one order, even when the customer double-clicks or the network drops replies
Never lose track of a payment: after a crash or a timeout the system must be able to find out what really happened
Every amount in the books must balance, and past records are never edited
Stay correct before staying fast: a payment can take a few seconds, but it must not be wrong
Keep card numbers out of the shop's own systems as far as possible
Keep taking orders when the payment provider is slow or down

firstAttempt.text: One server. When the customer presses Pay, the server calls the payment provider and waits for the answer. If the provider says yes, it sets the order's paid column to true, and if it says no, it shows an error. It is short, and for a small shop it mostly works.
limits: If the provider's reply never arrives, the server does not know whether the card was charged, and a retry can charge it again
A double-click or a browser refresh sends the same request twice
A single paid flag says nothing about how much was charged, refunded or fees taken
The server may crash between the provider's yes and saving the result, so a paid customer sees an unpaid order
A slow provider ties up every web request waiting for it

steps.title: Give every payment attempt an idempotency key
steps.problem: When a reply is lost, the caller cannot tell a charge that failed from a charge that worked, and a retry or a double-click can charge twice.
steps.fix: The checkout page makes up a unique key for each payment attempt and sends it with the request. The API saves the key and the payment in its own database before it calls the provider, and passes the same key on to the provider. A repeated request with a known key returns the stored result instead of starting a new charge, and the provider does the same on its side.
steps.tradeoff: Retrying becomes safe, which makes every other failure easier to handle. The key has to be generated once per attempt and not per click, stored for long enough, and checked against the amount, or a reused key with different details could be mistaken for a repeat.

steps.title: Model a payment as a state machine and wait for the provider's webhook
steps.problem: A timeout leaves the outcome unknown, and holding a web request open while a bank decides ties up the server.
steps.fix: A payment moves through states: created, processing, then succeeded or failed, with an unknown state after a timeout. Only listed moves are allowed. The API answers 'processing' and the final result arrives as a signed webhook from the provider (a message it sends to our server), which the handler checks and applies with a conditional update (it only applies if the payment is still in the expected state). If no webhook comes, a job asks the provider for the payment's status by its key.
steps.tradeoff: The server never guesses and never blocks for long, and an unknown outcome is settled by the provider's own record. The customer may see a brief 'processing' screen, webhooks can arrive late, twice or out of order, and each one must be safe to apply again.

steps.title: Record money in an append-only double-entry ledger
steps.problem: A single 'paid' flag or balance column cannot explain how much was charged, refunded or taken as fees, and edits to it erase the history.
steps.fix: Every movement of money writes two ledger entries in one database transaction (all-or-nothing), a debit on one account and a credit on another for the same amount, such as customer payment against shop revenue. Entries are never edited. A refund is a new pair of entries that reverses part of the old pair. Amounts are whole numbers of the smallest currency unit, never floating-point numbers, and every account's balance is the sum of its entries.
steps.tradeoff: The books always balance, and any number can be traced to the events that made it. Balances need summing or a maintained running total, and a transactional SQL database is the natural home because this is one place where strict ACID guarantees are worth their cost.

steps.title: Publish payment events through a transactional outbox
steps.problem: The order system must hear about every payment result, but telling it directly can fail after the money has already moved.
steps.fix: In the same transaction that writes the ledger entries, the service also writes an event row to an outbox table (events waiting to be published). A relay process reads the outbox and publishes each event to a stream, where the order, email and accounting services consume it. Consumers treat an event they have seen before as a no-op.
steps.tradeoff: An event is published if and only if the payment was recorded, so nothing is lost and nothing is announced that did not happen. Delivery is at least once, so consumers must be idempotent, and the order may be confirmed a moment after the payment.

steps.title: Reconcile the ledger against the provider every day
steps.problem: Bugs, missed webhooks and manual changes can leave the shop's records disagreeing with what the provider and the bank actually did.
steps.fix: Each day the provider sends a settlement report listing every charge, refund and fee. A reconciliation job matches each line to a ledger payment by its key and amount, and raises an alert for anything missing on either side, with a different amount, or in a different state. Differences are corrected with new ledger entries, never by editing old ones.
steps.tradeoff: Errors that slip past every other defence are found within a day, and finance gets a verified record. It is a batch process that finds problems after the fact, and someone has to own the exceptions queue.

steps.title: Keep card data out, and score each payment for fraud
steps.problem: Handling raw card numbers brings heavy security rules and a very attractive target, and criminals test stolen cards in bulk.
steps.fix: The checkout page uses a card form served by the provider, so the card number goes straight to the provider over an encrypted TLS connection and the shop only receives a token. The API stores that token, never the number. Each payment is scored for fraud before it is sent, with rate limits per customer, card and address, and risky ones are declined or sent for extra verification. Provider credentials live in a secrets manager.
steps.tradeoff: The shop's systems never hold card numbers, which removes most of the compliance work and the worst breach. The shop depends on the provider's form and tokens, and fraud rules always trade lost sales against lost money.

failures.scenario: The provider charges the card but its reply is lost
failures.impact: The shop does not know whether the customer paid, and a second charge would take their money twice.
failures.answer: The payment stays in processing or unknown. A retry uses the same idempotency key, so the provider returns the existing charge. If retries keep failing, the provider's webhook or a status query settles it, and the customer sees 'processing' rather than an error.

failures.scenario: The payment provider is down or very slow
failures.impact: Checkout requests pile up waiting for an answer, which could take down the whole shop.
failures.answer: Calls to the provider have a short timeout and sit behind a circuit breaker, so the shop fails fast instead of piling up. The checkout shows a clear message and keeps the cart, or switches to a second provider where one is configured. Payments left in processing are picked up by the status job once the provider recovers.

failures.scenario: The same webhook is delivered twice, or an old one arrives after a newer one
failures.impact: A refund could be applied twice, or a succeeded payment could be set back to processing.
failures.answer: The handler checks the webhook's signature, then makes only allowed state changes with conditional updates, so a repeat or an out-of-date event changes nothing. Each event id is recorded when it is handled.

failures.scenario: The server crashes after the provider says yes but before the ledger is written
failures.impact: The customer has paid and the shop has no record of it.
failures.answer: The payment was stored in processing before the call, so a recovery job finds it, asks the provider for its status by key, and completes the ledger entries and the outbox event in one transaction. Reconciliation the next day would catch it otherwise.

alternatives.title: When the customer learns the result

options.name: Wait for the provider inside the request
options.pro: Simple to build, and the customer sees the result straight away
options.con: Ties up servers, and a timeout leaves the customer with no answer

options.name: Answer 'processing' and confirm by webhook
options.pro: Handles slow banks and 3-D Secure steps (an extra check such as a code sent to the phone), and survives timeouts cleanly
options.con: More states and a page that updates itself

alternatives.pick: Return quickly and confirm by webhook. A short wait inside the request is fine as long as the webhook remains the source of truth.

alternatives.title: How to store balances

options.name: A balance column that is updated
options.pro: Trivial to read and to write
options.con: No history, silent errors, and nothing to check it against

options.name: Append-only double-entry ledger
options.pro: Always balances, fully traceable, and refunds and fees are more entries
options.con: Balances are sums, and the design needs more care up front

options.name: A full event-sourced payment history
options.pro: Every state change is kept and can be replayed
options.con: More machinery than most shops need

alternatives.pick: A double-entry ledger from the first day. It is cheap to add early and very hard to bolt on later.

alternatives.title: Who handles card data

options.name: The shop stores and sends card numbers
options.con: The heaviest security and compliance duties, and the biggest breach risk

options.name: Provider-hosted card form and tokens
options.pro: Card numbers never reach the shop's servers
options.con: Tied to the provider's form and tokens, which limits moving to another

options.name: Provider-hosted full checkout page
options.pro: Least work and the smallest scope
options.con: Least control over the look and the flow

alternatives.pick: A provider-hosted card form with tokens. Build a custom card vault only at a scale where fees justify the compliance cost.

alternatives.title: Keeping the order and the payment consistent

options.name: One database transaction across both
options.con: Only works if they share a database, and not at all with an outside provider

options.name: Two-phase commit between services
options.con: Providers do not take part, and a stuck coordinator blocks everything

options.name: Events with an outbox and compensating steps (such as a refund that undoes an earlier step)
options.pro: Works across services and providers, and recovers from crashes
options.con: The two are briefly out of step, and refunds are separate steps

alternatives.pick: Events through an outbox with compensating actions such as refunds. It is the only option that works with an outside provider.

roles.label: Customer side
roles.description: The checkout page and the provider's card form.

roles.label: Entry points
roles.description: The payment API, webhook handler and card form.

roles.label: Services
roles.description: The provider, fraud checks, reconciliation and order handling.

quiz.question: A shop's server calls the payment provider to charge a card, and the call times out after 10 seconds with no reply. The server cannot tell whether the card was charged. What should happen next?
options: Mark the payment as failed and show an error, so the customer presses Pay again and a new attempt starts with a freshly generated key.
Retry with the idempotency key that was saved before the first call, so the provider returns the original charge, not a new one.
Wait 30 seconds and send the charge again with a newly generated idempotency key, since a timeout usually means the first request never arrived.
Mark the order as paid right away and let the daily settlement report from the provider correct any charge that did not go through.
quiz.explanation: The key was saved before the first call, so a retry with it is safe: the provider either returns the charge that already happened or creates it once. A new key makes the retry a second charge and can take the money twice. Marking the payment failed has the same flaw as soon as the customer tries again. Marking the order paid is a guess that ships goods for money that may never arrive.

quiz.question: Peak load is 50 payments per second, and assume about half of them need a bank verification step that takes up to 60 seconds. The web tier has 200 worker threads, and each checkout request stays open until the provider answers. What is the right change?
options: Raise the web tier to 1,500 worker threads, so every waiting request has its own thread and matches the 25 slow payments started each second, with some headroom.
Cut the provider timeout to 5 seconds and treat a timeout as a declined payment, so threads are released quickly and customers can try again straight away.
Hand each payment to a queue with 200 consumers that each wait for the provider's answer, so the web tier can respond to the browser immediately.
Reply 'processing' straight away and finish through a signed provider webhook, with a job that asks the provider for the status of any payment still waiting.
quiz.explanation: Holding a request open for up to 60 seconds needs about 1,500 threads at this rate, and a timeout does not mean a decline. Answering 'processing' and settling by webhook, with a status job as backup, frees the threads and keeps the provider as the source of truth. A queue of 200 blocking consumers has the same limit, only moved.

quiz.question: After the ledger transaction commits, the payment service publishes a 'payment succeeded' event to a message broker in a separate call. Once a month the service crashes between the commit and the publish, and an order stays unpaid although the customer was charged. What is the best fix?
options: Write the event to an outbox in the same transaction as the ledger entries, and let a relay publish it at least once to idempotent consumers.
Publish the event first and commit the ledger entries afterwards, so the order service always hears about the payment before anything else can fail.
Wrap the ledger database, the broker and the payment provider in a two-phase commit, so that all three either commit together or abort together.
Publish inside a loop of 5 attempts with backoff right after the commit, since the broker is usually only briefly down.
quiz.explanation: Writing the event in the same transaction means it exists if and only if the payment was recorded, and the relay keeps trying until it is published. Publishing first can announce a payment that then fails to commit. A retry loop in memory dies with the process, and a payment provider cannot take part in a two-phase commit.
